Raymond III was born around 1140.
He was the son of Raymond II Count of Tripoli and Hodierna of Jerusalem.
His father Raymond II was killed in 1152.
After the assassination Raymond III inherited the county while still a minor.
He ruled under the regency of his mother Hodierna and later under the influence of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
*Early Life and Accession*
Raymond III received training in knightly arts and learned the politics of the Crusader states.
He married Eschiva of Ibelin in 1165 strengthening ties with the powerful Ibelin family.
The marriage brought him support from the barons of Jerusalem and helped secure his position.
During his youth he faced internal strife as rival nobles challenged his authority.
He managed to maintain control by balancing loyalties between the King of Jerusalem and the local nobility.
*Military Campaigns and Alliances*
Raymond III participated in the campaigns of King Amalric I against Egypt.
He took part in the siege of Bilbeis in 1168 and contributed troops to the effort.
In 1171 he joined the expedition to support the Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos against Seljuk threats.
His diplomatic skill was evident when he negotiated truces with Muslim leaders to protect trade routes.
He allied with the Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller to defend the northern frontier.
Raymond III also negotiated with Saladin seeking to avoid open conflict while preparing for defense.
*Later Years and Death*
By the late 1170s tensions rose as Saladin unified Muslim lands and threatened the Crusader states.
Raymond III tried to mediate between the factions of the Kingdom of Jerusalem but his efforts were often ignored.
He opposed the aggressive policies of Guy of Lusignan who became king through marriage to Sibylla.
When Guy led the Crusader army to the disastrous Battle of Hattin in 1187 Raymond III was absent from the field.
His absence has been debated by historians some argue he withdrew in protest others claim he was ill.
After the defeat at Hattin the county of Tripoli fell to Saladin in 1189.
Raymond III died shortly thereafter in 1189 possibly from wounds or illness.
His legacy is mixed he is remembered as a capable administrator a shrewd diplomat and a lord who struggled to unite the fractious Crusader nobility.
The county of Tripoli remained under Muslim control until the later Crusades briefly revived Christian rule.
